Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Learning agency combines producing outputs with learning
kp.d: Roberts and Forsyth define learning agency as simultaneously completing work and learning through its production. Roberts describes observing some AI users shortcut understanding while others accelerate learning, attributing this difference to disposition rather than talent or technical background. Their account concerns AI-enabled learning and technical problem-solving rather than changes to legal-service delivery specifically.
qs: learning agency — the disposition to run two processes at once, producing the output AND learning from the production.
Some used them to shortcut understanding. Others used them to accelerate learning. And the difference wasn't talent or technical background — it was disposition.

kp.k: Conversational troubleshooting expands nontechnical users' capabilities
kp.d: Roberts reports using screenshots of errors and questions to Claude to identify problems, alternatives and workarounds. She attributes her ability to build complex analytical tools, development environments and deployment pipelines to this iterative approach, while explicitly distinguishing it from understanding all the technical details. This is a personal account of capability development, not a measured finding about users generally.
qs: I screenshot the error, put it into Claude, and ask: what does this mean? What else can we do? How else can I achieve my goal?
But I've used this approach to accomplish things that would previously have been completely outside my reach — complex analytical tools, development environments, deployment pipelines.
Not because I suddenly understood all of the technical details, but because I learned that things don't stop when the computer says no.

kp.k: Task decomposition resolved an output-limit obstacle
kp.d: The central anecdote concerns Forsyth applying Dragonfly agents and skills to academic work and encountering Claude's 32000 output token maximum. Roberts recommended breaking the requested work into smaller tasks; Forsyth reports that Claude subsequently diagnosed the same problem and proposed the same fix. A few days later, Forsyth reported creating a new tool without asking Roberts questions. The authors present this sequence as an illustration of learning agency.
qs: API Error: Claude's response exceeded the 32000 output token maximum.
the token limit was too low for the output being requested
breaking up the task into smaller parts so that Claude could complete individual tasks under the limit.
When I took it back to Claude and asked, Claude diagnosed the same problem and suggested the same fix.
A few days later I called Anthea to say that I had created a new tool all by myself, without needing her to answer a single question.

kp.k: Learning agency requires time as well as disposition
kp.d: Forsyth qualifies Roberts's initial interpretation of her request for help: she was following agents Roberts had designed and explained, so was oriented toward learning from Roberts, and she was fitting the task among other work. She argues that bandwidth for exploration and trial and error is a condition of learning agency, not merely an individual's willingness to learn.
qs: I was therefore oriented towards learning from Anthea, rather than the machine.
Learning agency requires bandwidth, not just disposition.
It's very hard to open yourself to new learning when you feel you have absolutely no time for exploration and trial and error.

kp.k: Revised helplessness theory makes control the learned response
kp.d: The authors recount Seligman's 1967 experiments in which animals exposed to inescapable shocks stopped attempting escape even when escape became possible, and his application of learned helplessness to human depression. They then report Maier and Seligman's revised neuroscience account, citing their 2016 paper: passivity under prolonged aversive events is the default, whereas control must be learned through experiencing a connection between action and changed outcomes. This reported theoretical mechanism supplies the framework for their AI-use argument.
qs: Seligman coined the term learned helplessness in 1967 after experiments showing that animals exposed to inescapable shocks eventually stopped trying to escape — even when escape became possible.
Seligman used this to explain depression in humans: repeated exposure to uncontrollable events teaches passivity.
Passivity, it turns out, is the default neurological response to prolonged aversive events. It doesn't need to be learned.
What does need to be learned — actively, through experience — is control.
The brain has to develop the circuit that detects contingency: the connection between "I did something" and "something changed."

kp.k: Opaque computing denied users experiences of effective control
kp.d: Applying the revised theory to computing, the authors argue that opaque errors, engineer-oriented interfaces and an inability to question machines left nontechnical users accepting failure, seeking expert help or giving up. They reinterpret their own passivity as a lack of experiences establishing effective control rather than something actively learned. This is the authors' theoretical analogy, not a reported study of computer users.
qs: Opaque error messages with no explanation. Interfaces designed for engineers. No way to ask "why?"
The error was a wall. You accepted it and called someone who knew more than you did. Or you gave up.
We didn't learn to be passive around computers. We simply never had the experience of contingency that would have built the alternative.

kp.k: AI enables agency only through active experimentation
kp.d: The authors argue that AI turns errors into opportunities for dialogue, but does not automatically produce agency: users must initiate questions, try alternatives and observe outcomes. They interpret Forsyth's experience as a shift in default response rather than competence, and recommend treating subsequent obstacles as conversation starters. Their proposed mechanism is repeated experience of successful action, which they describe as learning control.
qs: AI changes this — but only if you ask.
It creates the possibility of a conversation with the error.
But you have to be the one who starts the conversation.
learning agency is an action, not a belief.
Miranda's shift wasn't from incompetence to competence — she was always competent.
And it's learned through the experience of contingency: doing something, seeing it work, and doing it again.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts and Forsyth claim that conversational AI enables non-technical users to troubleshoot obstacles, undertake previously inaccessible technical work, and learn through producing outputs.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain account of AI-assisted learning, academic work and software development, not a claim about legal-service delivery or legal markets. The authors argue that AI changes error messages from stopping points into opportunities to ask questions, explore alternatives and exercise control. Roberts reports using Claude-assisted troubleshooting to build technical systems despite not being a software engineer. Forsyth reports progressing from seeking Roberts's help to independently creating a tool. Their broader claim is that repeated experiences of successfully acting on AI guidance can change users' default responses to technical obstacles. They distinguish using AI to bypass understanding from using it to accelerate learning.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of the authors' first-person experiences and observations, supported by an analogy to cited psychological and neuroscience research.
pts.d: Roberts describes routinely submitting error screenshots to Claude and asking for explanations and workarounds. The central incident concerns Forsyth encountering Claude's 32,000-output-token limit while using Dragonfly agents for academic work. Roberts recommended splitting the task; Forsyth reports that Claude independently diagnosed the same issue and suggested the same remedy. Forsyth subsequently reported creating a new tool without Roberts's assistance. The authors invoke Seligman and Maier's 1967 research and their 2016 reconsideration of learned helplessness to explain how experiencing control might alter responses to computers. These references supply the authors' conceptual basis, rather than direct experimental evidence about AI users. The document provides no systematic AI-user study, benchmark, quantified productivity result or neurological measurement supporting its application of this theory.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern capabilities and behavioural changes already experienced by April 2026, conditional on active questioning, experimentation and available time.
pts.d: The narrative describes events in the week preceding the April 2026 publication and a follow-up a few days after the troubleshooting incident; it offers no dated future forecast. The authors argue that AI's availability alone does not generate agency: users must initiate questions, try alternatives and experience their actions changing outcomes. Forsyth qualifies the initial emphasis on disposition by stressing bandwidth and time for exploration. She also explains that she initially sought Roberts's help because she was following agents Roberts had designed and explained. For the specific token-limit problem, the proposed workaround was to divide the requested output into smaller tasks that fit within the limit.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected group is non-technical computer users, illustrated by two law, regulation and governance academics building an AI-enabled platform.
pts.d: Roberts and Forsyth present themselves as domain experts without technology backgrounds who learned AI through building Dragonfly Thinking. Their account suggests that similarly situated users can gain technical capability, learn while completing work, and become less dependent on more technically experienced colleagues for troubleshooting. Forsyth's academic work provides a concrete setting. The source does not identify effects on law-firm staffing, legal fees, clients, legal-service providers or access to justice; its authors' legal backgrounds do not make these claims legal-market predictions.
